questions.source_name: NSEJS / Junior Science Biology · Q01 · MODEL · D2 (Score 4)
questions.stem:
In sweet pea (*Lathyrus odoratus*), purple flower coloration requires functional enzymes produced by two independently assorting dominant alleles, $C$ and $P$. Plants with genotypes $C\_pp, ccP\_,$ or $ccpp$ produce white flowers due to a biochemical pathway block.
[FIG-stem-bio-complementary-genes-pathway]
Two dihybrid heterozygous purple-flowered plants ($CcPp \times CcPp$) are crossed, yielding 1600 viable seeds. Determine the expected phenotypic ratio of Purple to White flowers in the progeny, and calculate the minimum total number of meiotic divisions required in the parent plants to produce the male and female gametes that formed these 1600 seeds.
questions.figure_note: Complementary gene metabolic pathway and megasporogenesis vs microsporogenesis meiosis stoichiometry.

hints.prompt: H1 (Complementary Gene Phenotype): Group the 16 Punnett square classes by flower color.
hints.text: Only genotypes with at least one C and one P (C_P_) produce purple flowers (9/16). All other classes (3 C_pp + 3 ccP_ + 1 ccpp = 7/16) produce white flowers.

hints.prompt: H2 (Male Gamete Meiosis): How many pollen grains are produced per meiotic division?
hints.text: In plants, 1 microspore mother cell yields 4 functional pollen grains. For 1600 pollen grains: 1600 / 4 = 400 meiotic divisions.

hints.prompt: H3 (Crux Move): Account for functional female gametes and sum.
hints.text: Crux Move: Each megaspore mother cell yields 4 megaspores, but 3 degenerate, leaving only 1 functional megaspore per meiosis (1600 divisions). Total = 400 + 1600 = 2000.

questions.answer: Official Key: (A) Ratio = 9 : 7; Total meiotic divisions = 2000
steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Dihybrid cross CcPp x CcPp in sweet pea produces 1600 seeds. C and P are complementary dominant alleles. We find phenotypic ratio and required meiotic divisions.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Genotype distribution: 9 C_P_ : 3 C_pp : 3 ccP_ : 1 ccpp. Only C_P_ has both functional enzymes for anthocyanin (9 Purple : 7 White). For 1600 seeds, 1600 pollen grains and 1600 functional ovules are required.
3. Execution & Resolution: Pollen divisions = 1600 / 4 = 400. Ovule divisions = 1600 / 1 = 1600 (due to 3 degenerating megaspores). Total meiotic divisions = 400 + 1600 = 2000. Option A.
questions.check: Independent check: If female gametes also yielded 4 functional spores, total would be 400 + 400 = 800 (Option B distractor). Botanical fact confirms 3 degenerate, requiring 1600 MMC divisions. Total = 2000. Confirmed.

questions.source_name: NSEJS / Junior Science Biology · Q02 · MODEL · D2 (Score 4)
questions.stem: During the generation and propagation of a nerve impulse along an unmyelinated mammalian axon, which sequence of ionic events across the axonal membrane correctly describes the transition from resting potential ($-70\text{ mV}$) through peak depolarization ($+30\text{ mV}$) to repolarization and the refractory period?
options: A: Threshold depolarization to -55 mV triggers rapid opening of voltage-gated Na+ channels causing Na+ influx to +30 mV; at peak, Na+ channels inactivate and voltage-gated K+ channels open causing K+ efflux to repolarize and briefly hyperpolarize the membrane (-90 mV) before Na+/K+ ATPase restores resting potential.
B: Influx of K+ ions causes depolarization to +30 mV, followed by efflux of Na+ ions during repolarization.
C: Opening of Cl- channels depolarizes the membrane to +30 mV, while opening of Ca2+ channels repolarizes it.
D: The Na+/K+ pump reverses its direction during an action potential, pumping 3 K+ in and 2 Na+ out.

hints.prompt: H1 (Threshold and Depolarization): Which ion moves down its electrochemical gradient to drive the membrane potential positive?
hints.text: Voltage-gated Na+ channels open rapidly at threshold (-55 mV), driving rapid Na+ influx toward the sodium equilibrium potential (+60 mV), peaking at +30 mV.

hints.prompt: H2 (Repolarization Mechanism): Which channel opens to bring the potential back toward negative values?
hints.text: At +30 mV, Na+ channels inactivate and slower voltage-gated K+ channels open, allowing rapid K+ efflux down its concentration gradient.

hints.prompt: H3 (Crux Move): Trace after-hyperpolarization and resting potential recovery.
hints.text: Crux Move: K+ channels close slowly causing temporary hyperpolarization (-90 mV), and the Na+/K+ ATPase restores original resting ion distributions (3 Na+ out, 2 K+ in).

questions.answer: Official Key: (A) Threshold depolarization to -55 mV triggers rapid opening of voltage-gated Na+ channels causing Na+ influx to +30 mV; at peak, Na+ channels inactivate and voltage-gated K+ channels open causing K+ efflux to repolarize and briefly hyperpolarize the membrane (-90 mV) before Na+/K+ ATPase restores resting potential.
steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: The axonal membrane maintains resting potential at -70 mV via Na+/K+ ATPase (3 Na+ pumped out for 2 K+ pumped in) and K+ leak channels. We evaluate action potential phases.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Depolarization reaching threshold (-55 mV) triggers voltage-gated Na+ activation gates, driving massive Na+ influx down concentration and electrical gradients to +30 mV.

3. Execution & Resolution: At +30 mV, Na+ inactivation gates close, and voltage-gated K+ channels open, causing rapid K+ efflux that repolarizes the axon. Delayed closure of K+ channels produces after-hyperpolarization (-90 mV) until active Na+/K+ pumping re-establishes -70 mV. Option A.
questions.check: Independent check: Intracellular [K+] is ~140 mM vs extracellular 5 mM; [Na+] is 145 mM extracellular vs 12 mM intracellular. Na+ influx depolarizes; K+ efflux repolarizes. Option A confirmed.

questions.source_name: NSEJS / Junior Science Biology · Q03 · APPLY · D2 (Score 3)
questions.stem: A person accidentally touches a hot stove with their finger and immediately withdraws their hand before feeling conscious pain. Which sequence correctly represents the neural pathway and neurotransmitter action governing this monosynaptic/polysynaptic spinal reflex arc?
options: A: Thermal pain nociceptor -> Afferent sensory neuron via dorsal root ganglion -> Spinal cord gray matter interneuron -> Efferent motor neuron via ventral root -> Acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junction causing biceps contraction.
B: Pain nociceptor -> Cerebral cortex primary sensory area -> Motor cortex -> Descending pyramidal tract -> Efferent motor neuron.
C: Afferent sensory neuron via ventral root -> Sympathetic ganglion -> Adrenal medulla -> Motor nerve via dorsal root.
D: Interneuron in cerebellum -> Ventral horn sensory cell -> Dorsal root motor nerve -> Neuromuscular junction.

hints.prompt: H1 (Root Anatomy of Spinal Cord): Remember Bell-Magendie Law for spinal roots.
hints.text: Sensory afferent fibers enter the spinal cord via the dorsal root (cell bodies in dorsal root ganglion). Motor efferent fibers exit via the ventral root.

hints.prompt: H2 (Spinal Reflex Architecture): Does the initial withdrawal reflex involve cerebral cortex processing?
hints.text: No; spinal reflex arcs are integrated at the level of spinal cord interneurons to minimize response time before ascending tracts inform the sensory cortex.

hints.prompt: H3 (Crux Move): Trace the somatic neurotransmitter at the neuromuscular junction.
hints.text: Crux Move: Somatic motor neurons release acetylcholine (ACh) onto nicotinic receptors on the motor end-plate of the effector muscle (biceps).

questions.answer: Official Key: (A) Thermal pain nociceptor -> Afferent sensory neuron via dorsal root ganglion -> Spinal cord gray matter interneuron -> Efferent motor neuron via ventral root -> Acetylcholine release at neuromuscular junction causing biceps contraction.
steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Rapid hand withdrawal from a noxious thermal stimulus occurs via a polysynaptic spinal withdrawal reflex arc.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Thermal nociceptors generate action potentials in pseudo-unipolar sensory neurons entering the spinal cord through the dorsal root ganglion. In the dorsal horn gray matter, they synapse onto excitatory interneurons.

3. Execution & Resolution: The interneuron excites alpha-motor neurons whose axons exit through the ventral root. At the motor end plate, action potentials trigger voltage-gated Ca2+ entry, exocytosis of acetylcholine, and rapid contraction of the flexor muscle. Option A.
questions.check: Independent check: Dorsal = Sensory, Ventral = Motor (Bell-Magendie law). Conscious perception reaches cortex via spinothalamic tract only after the spinal reflex completes. Confirmed.

questions.source_name: NSEJS / Junior Science Biology · Q04 · JUSTIFY · D2 (Score 4)
questions.stem: When a potted seedling is placed horizontally in the dark, the shoot bends upwards (negative gravitropism) while the primary root bends downwards (positive gravitropism). According to the Cholodny-Went hypothesis and tissue-specific auxin dose-response kinetics, which physiological mechanism accounts for these opposite directional responses?
options: A: Statolith sedimentation causes auxin to accumulate along the lower side of both root and shoot; this high auxin concentration stimulates cell elongation in the shoot, but exceeds the optimum threshold in the root, thereby inhibiting lower-side root cell elongation.
B: Auxin accumulates exclusively on the upper side of roots and the lower side of shoots.
C: Gibberellin replaces auxin in roots to reverse the gravitational bending direction.
D: Ethylene production on the upper side of the root accelerates cell division while auxin has no effect.

hints.prompt: H1 (Auxin Redistribution by Gravity): How does gravity affect auxin distribution in horizontal organs?
hints.text: Dense starch-filled amyloplasts (statoliths) sediment to the lower side of cells, stimulating polar PIN-transporter localization that moves auxin to the lower flank in both roots and shoots.

hints.prompt: H2 (Sensitivity Curves of Roots vs Shoots): Compare the optimum auxin concentrations for elongation.
hints.text: Roots are roughly 100,000 times more sensitive to auxin than shoots. The optimal auxin concentration for shoot elongation is ~10^-5 M, whereas for roots it is ~10^-10 M.

hints.prompt: H3 (Crux Move): Reconcile the differential elongation responses.
hints.text: Crux Move: High auxin on the lower flank stimulates shoot cell elongation (bending upward), but suppresses root cell elongation (causing the upper side to elongate faster and bend downward).

questions.answer: Official Key: (A) Statolith sedimentation causes auxin to accumulate along the lower side of both root and shoot; this high auxin concentration stimulates cell elongation in the shoot, but exceeds the optimum threshold in the root, thereby inhibiting lower-side root cell elongation.
steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: A seedling placed horizontally displays negative gravitropism in shoots and positive gravitropism in roots despite identical lateral gravity vectors.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Statoliths sediment to the bottom of statocytes in shoot endodermis and root columella, redirecting PIN efflux carriers to transport auxin (IAA) laterally to the lower flank of both organs.

3. Execution & Resolution: Shoots have a high auxin tolerance; the accumulated lower-flank auxin accelerates proton extrusion (acid growth), causing the lower side to elongate faster than the upper side (upward curvature). Roots operate at much lower sensitivity thresholds; the same high auxin concentration induces ethylene/growth arrest on the lower flank, so the upper flank elongates faster (downward curvature). Option A.
questions.check: Independent check: Classical Thimann auxin dose-response curve shows stimulation for shoots at concentrations that are deeply inhibitory for roots. Option A confirmed.

questions.source_name: NSEJS / Junior Science Biology · Q05 · MODEL · D2 (Score 4)
questions.stem: A short-day plant (SDP) with a critical dark period of $9.0\text{ hours}$ is exposed to a light regimen of $14\text{ hours light}$ and $10\text{ hours darkness}$. In one experiment, the $10\text{ hour}$ dark phase is interrupted in the middle by a $2\text{ minute}$ flash of red light ($660\text{ nm}$). In a second experiment, this red flash is immediately followed by a $2\text{ minute}$ flash of far-red light ($730\text{ nm}$). What are the flowering responses in the two experiments?
options: A: Experiment 1: Fails to flower; Experiment 2: Flowers successfully
B: Experiment 1: Flowers successfully; Experiment 2: Fails to flower
C: Both experiments fail to flower

hints.prompt: H1 (Requirement for SDP Flowering): What governs flowering in short-day plants?
hints.text: Short-day plants are actually 'long-night plants'; they require a continuous, uninterrupted dark period equal to or exceeding the critical night length (here 9.0 h).

hints.prompt: H2 (Phytochrome Interconversion): What happens when phytochrome absorbs red (660 nm) vs far-red (730 nm) light?
hints.text: Red light (660 nm) converts inactive Pr into active Pfr. Pfr inhibits flowering in short-day plants. Far-red light (730 nm) converts Pfr back into inactive Pr.

hints.prompt: H3 (Crux Move): Determine the final phytochrome form in both experiments.
hints.text: Crux Move: In Exp 1, the night break leaves Pfr, preventing flowering. In Exp 2, the subsequent far-red flash photoreverses Pfr back to Pr, resetting the dark clock and permitting flowering.

questions.answer: Official Key: (A) Experiment 1: Fails to flower; Experiment 2: Flowers successfully
steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: An SDP requires >= 9.0 h continuous uninterrupted darkness. The baseline provides 10.0 h darkness (> 9.0 h).

2. Physical Model & Formulation: A brief flash of red light (660 nm) converts inactive Pr into active Pfr. In SDPs, presence of Pfr during the critical night suppresses florigen synthesis, aborting flowering (Experiment 1 fails).

3. Execution & Resolution: When red light is immediately followed by far-red light (730 nm), Pfr is photoconverted back into Pr. Because the final light signal is far-red, no active Pfr remains to inhibit flowering, allowing the plant to flower (Experiment 2 succeeds). Option A.
questions.check: Independent check: Classic Borthwick-Hendricks phytochrome photoreversibility: the wavelength of the final flash determines the biological response. Final far-red = Pr active state = flowering in SDPs. Confirmed.

questions.source_name: NSEJS / Junior Science Biology · Q06 · SYNTHESIZE · D2 (Score 5)
questions.stem: Following a carbohydrate-rich meal, human blood glucose rises from baseline ($90\text{ mg/dL}$) to $150\text{ mg/dL}$, triggering endocrine secretion. Later during fasting, glucose falls to $70\text{ mg/dL}$. Which statement correctly identifies the pancreatic endocrine cell types, their secreted hormones, and their primary biochemical target mechanisms during these two physiological states?
options: A: Hyperglycemia stimulates pancreatic beta-cells to secrete insulin, promoting GLUT-4 translocation, hepatic glycogenesis, and cellular glucose uptake; hypoglycemia stimulates alpha-cells to secrete glucagon, activating hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
B: Hyperglycemia stimulates alpha-cells to secrete insulin, while hypoglycemia stimulates beta-cells to secrete glucagon.
C: Insulin activates glycogenolysis in skeletal muscle to release free glucose into the blood stream.
D: Glucagon directly stimulates adipocytes to absorb excess circulating glucose as triglycerides.

hints.prompt: H1 (Islet of Langerhans Cell Types): Distinguish beta-cells from alpha-cells.
hints.text: Beta-cells produce insulin in response to elevated blood glucose. Alpha-cells produce glucagon in response to low blood glucose.

hints.prompt: H2 (Cellular Action of Insulin): How does insulin facilitate glucose entry into muscle and fat?
hints.text: Insulin receptor activation stimulates intracellular vesicles containing GLUT-4 glucose transporters to fuse with the plasma membrane.

hints.prompt: H3 (Crux Move): Contrast hepatic glycogenolysis with glycogenesis.
hints.text: Crux Move: Insulin triggers glycogenesis in liver and muscles; glucagon acts on liver hepatocytes to stimulate glycogen breakdown (glycogenolysis) and gluconeogenesis.

questions.answer: Official Key: (A) Hyperglycemia stimulates pancreatic beta-cells to secrete insulin, promoting GLUT-4 translocation, hepatic glycogenesis, and cellular glucose uptake; hypoglycemia stimulates alpha-cells to secrete glucagon, activating hepatic glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Blood glucose homeostasis oscillates between post-prandial hyperglycemia (150 mg/dL) and fasting hypoglycemia (70 mg/dL).

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Elevated blood glucose is detected by beta-cells in the Islets of Langerhans, stimulating exocytosis of insulin. Insulin promotes glucose uptake via GLUT-4 translocation in skeletal muscle/adipose tissue and promotes glycogen synthesis (glycogenesis) in hepatocytes.

3. Execution & Resolution: In hypoglycemia, alpha-cells secrete glucagon. Glucagon binds GPCRs on hepatocytes, raising cAMP to activate glycogen phosphorylase (glycogenolysis) and gluconeogenic enzymes, restoring circulating glucose to 90 mg/dL. Option A.
questions.check: Independent check: Muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so muscle glycogen cannot be released directly into blood (refuting distractor C). Glucagon raises blood glucose (refuting D). Option A confirmed.

questions.stem: Red-green color blindness is an X-linked recessive condition ($X^c$). A man with normal color vision ($X^C Y$) marries a woman with normal vision whose father was color-blind ($X^c Y$). If this couple has four children (two sons and two daughters), what is the probability that their first son will be color-blind, and what is the probability that any given daughter will be color-blind?
options: A: Probability for a son = 50.0%; Probability for a daughter = 0.0%
B: Probability for a son = 25.0%; Probability for a daughter = 25.0%
C: Probability for a son = 50.0%; Probability for a daughter = 50.0%
D: Probability for a son = 100.0%; Probability for a daughter = 0.0%

hints.prompt: H1 (Genotype of the Mother): Deduce the mother's genotype from her father's phenotype.
hints.text: The mother has normal vision but inherited an X chromosome from her color-blind father (X^c Y), so she must be a heterozygous carrier: X^C X^c.

hints.prompt: H2 (Sons' Inheritance): Which sex chromosome does a son inherit from each parent?
hints.text: A son inherits Y from the normal father and either X^C or X^c from the mother with 50% probability.

hints.prompt: H3 (Crux Move): Daughters' inheritance and phenotype.
hints.text: Crux Move: Every daughter receives X^C from the father. Because X^C is dominant, 100% of daughters have normal color vision (probability of affected daughter = 0.0%).

questions.answer: Official Key: (A) Probability for a son = 50.0%; Probability for a daughter = 0.0%
steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Father has genotype X^C Y. Mother has normal vision with a color-blind father (X^c Y), establishing her carrier genotype as X^C X^c.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Cross is X^C Y x X^C X^c. Male progeny genotypes: 1/2 X^C Y (normal vision), 1/2 X^c Y (color-blind). Female progeny genotypes: 1/2 X^C X^C (normal homozygous), 1/2 X^C X^c (normal carrier).

3. Execution & Resolution: For any given son, probability of color blindness is 1/2 = 50.0%. For any given daughter, because she always receives the dominant X^C allele from her father, probability of color blindness is 0.0%. Option A.
questions.check: Independent check: Sons inherit X strictly from mother; carrier mother gives 50% risk. Daughters inherit normal X from father, masking any maternal recessive allele. Option A confirmed.

questions.source_name: NSEJS / Junior Science Biology · Q08 · MODEL · D2 (Score 4)
questions.stem: A double-stranded DNA duplex contains 2000 base pairs ($4000$ total nucleotides). Biochemical analysis reveals that Adenine accounts for $28.0\%$ of the total nitrogenous bases in the molecule. Calculate the total number of Guanine nucleotides present in this DNA molecule and the total number of hydrogen bonds stabilizing the duplex.
options: A: Guanine nucleotides = 880; Total hydrogen bonds = 4880
B: Guanine nucleotides = 1120; Total hydrogen bonds = 5120
C: Guanine nucleotides = 880; Total hydrogen bonds = 5120
D: Guanine nucleotides = 440; Total hydrogen bonds = 4880

hints.prompt: H1 (Chargaff's Rules): Relate base proportions in double-stranded DNA.
hints.text: By Chargaff's rules, %A = %T and %G = %C. %A + %T + %G + %C = 100%.

hints.prompt: H2 (Count Guanine Bases): Calculate percentage and absolute count of Guanine.
hints.text: %A = 28% => %T = 28%. Total A+T = 56%. Remaining G+C = 44% => %G = 22%. Total nucleotides = 4000, so G = 0.22 * 4000 = 880.

hints.prompt: H3 (Crux Move): Calculate total hydrogen bonds in base pairs.
hints.text: Crux Move: A-T pairs have 2 hydrogen bonds; G-C pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds. Total H-bonds = 2 * (1120) + 3 * (880) = 2240 + 2640 = 4880.

questions.answer: Official Key: (A) Guanine nucleotides = 880; Total hydrogen bonds = 4880
steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: A 2000 bp (4000 nucleotides) double-stranded DNA molecule has 28.0% Adenine. We determine the count of Guanine and total hydrogen bonds.
2. Physical Model & Formulation: In dsDNA: [A] = [T] = 28.0% (1120 bases each, forming 1120 A-T base pairs). [G] = [C] = (100% - 56.0%) / 2 = 22.0% (880 bases each, forming 880 G-C base pairs).
3. Execution & Resolution: Count of Guanine = 880 nucleotides. Hydrogen bonds = 2 * (N_AT) + 3 * (N_GC) = 2 * 1120 + 3 * 880 = 2240 + 2640 = 4880 hydrogen bonds. Option A.
questions.check: Independent check: Total bp = 1120 + 880 = 2000 bp. H-bonds = 2240 + 2640 = 4880. Confirmed.

questions.source_name: NSEJS / Junior Science Biology · Q09 · JUSTIFY · D2 (Score 4)
questions.stem: Sickle-cell anemia is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a single base-pair substitution (point mutation) in the gene encoding the $\beta$-globin chain of hemoglobin. Which statement correctly identifies the nature of this mutation at the DNA, mRNA, and polypeptide levels, and explains why it causes sickling of erythrocytes under low oxygen tension?
options: A: A transversion point mutation replaces adenine with thymine in the coding strand (GAG -> GTG), producing a GUG codon in mRNA that substitutes polar, hydrophilic glutamic acid with non-polar, hydrophobic valine at position 6; under low pO2, deoxygenated HbS polymerizes into fibrous insoluble polymers that distort RBCs into sickle shapes.
B: A frameshift insertion of a single nucleotide disrupts the downstream reading frame, producing a truncated non-functional hemoglobin protein.
C: A transition mutation replaces cytosine with guanine (CTC -> CGC), producing an arginine substitution that prevents iron binding in the heme group.
D: A nonsense mutation introduces a premature stop codon (UAA) at position 6, terminating translation of the beta-globin chain.

hints.prompt: H1 (Mutation Classification): Is A -> T a transition or transversion?
hints.text: Purine (A) to pyrimidine (T) is a transversion mutation. Coding strand changes from GAG to GTG (template CTC to CAC).

hints.prompt: H2 (Codon and Amino Acid Shift): What amino acid does GUG encode?
hints.text: GAG encodes glutamic acid (negatively charged/hydrophilic). GUG encodes valine (hydrophobic/non-polar) at position 6 of the beta-chain.

hints.prompt: H3 (Crux Move): Hydrophobic interaction under deoxygenation.
hints.text: Crux Move: Deoxy-HbS exposes hydrophobic valine patches that adhere to complementary hydrophobic pockets on adjacent beta-chains, polymerizing into rigid fibers that sickle the cell.

questions.answer: Official Key: (A) A transversion point mutation replaces adenine with thymine in the coding strand (GAG -> GTG), producing a GUG codon in mRNA that substitutes polar, hydrophilic glutamic acid with non-polar, hydrophobic valine at position 6; under low pO2, deoxygenated HbS polymerizes into fibrous insoluble polymers that distort RBCs into sickle shapes.
steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Sickle-cell anemia is a classic monogenic hemoglobinopathy. We evaluate the molecular pathology at DNA, RNA, and protein tiers.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: Normal beta-globin gene has coding triplet GAG (template CTC), transcribed to GAG mRNA, specifying Glutamic acid (Glu) at position 6. In HbS, transversion A -> T yields GTG (template CAC), transcribed to GUG mRNA, specifying Valine (Val).

3. Execution & Resolution: Replacing hydrophilic glutamate with hydrophobic valine creates an abnormal sticky patch on the exterior surface of the deoxygenated hemoglobin tetramer, causing self-assembly into 14-strand helical filaments that mechanically deform erythrocytes into sickle shapes. Option A.
questions.check: Independent check: Purine <-> Pyrimidine is a transversion. Glu (polar acidic) -> Val (non-polar aliphatic) at position 6 of beta-globin chain is the textbook lesion for HbS. Option A confirmed.

questions.source_name: NSEJS / Junior Science Biology · Q10 · APPLY · D1 (Score 2)
questions.stem: Blood plasma calcium concentration is tightly maintained at approximately $9.0 - 11.0\text{ mg/dL}$ by the antagonistic actions of two peptide hormones: Parathyroid Hormone (PTH) and Calcitonin. Which of the following correctly pairs each hormone with its gland of origin, physiological trigger, and cellular action on bone and kidneys?
options: A: Hypocalcemia triggers the parathyroid glands to secrete PTH, which stimulates osteoclastic bone resorption and renal Ca2+ reabsorption; hypercalcemia triggers thyroid parafollicular C-cells to secrete calcitonin, which inhibits osteoclasts and promotes bone mineralization.
B: Hypercalcemia triggers parathyroid glands to secrete PTH to deposit excess calcium into bones; hypocalcemia triggers the thyroid gland to secrete calcitonin.
C: Both PTH and calcitonin are secreted by the adrenal cortex to regulate aldosterone and potassium channels.
D: Calcitonin stimulates renal synthesis of active Vitamin D (calcitriol) while PTH inhibits intestinal calcium absorption.

hints.prompt: H1 (Parathyroid Hormone Action): What is the physiological purpose of PTH?
hints.text: PTH is hypercalcemic (raises blood Ca2+). It is released in response to low plasma calcium (hypocalcemia).

hints.prompt: H2 (Calcitonin Action): What is the physiological purpose of Calcitonin?
hints.text: Calcitonin is hypocalcemic (lowers blood Ca2+). It is secreted by parafollicular C-cells of the thyroid gland in response to high plasma calcium.

hints.prompt: H3 (Crux Move): Target organs and cellular actions.
hints.text: Crux Move: PTH stimulates bone osteoclasts to dissolve hydroxyapatite and enhances renal Ca2+ reabsorption. Calcitonin inhibits osteoclasts and promotes Ca2+ excretion.

questions.answer: Official Key: (A) Hypocalcemia triggers the parathyroid glands to secrete PTH, which stimulates osteoclastic bone resorption and renal Ca2+ reabsorption; hypercalcemia triggers thyroid parafollicular C-cells to secrete calcitonin, which inhibits osteoclasts and promotes bone mineralization.
steps: 1. System Representation & Setup: Calcium homeostasis in human blood is regulated between 9-11 mg/dL by negative feedback loops involving PTH and calcitonin.

2. Physical Model & Formulation: When plasma Ca2+ drops below 9.0 mg/dL, chief cells in the parathyroid glands release PTH. PTH stimulates RANKL signaling to activate bone osteoclasts (releasing Ca2+ and phosphate), stimulates renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase to form calcitriol, and increases distal tubule Ca2+ reabsorption.

3. Execution & Resolution: Conversely, when plasma Ca2+ rises above 11.0 mg/dL, parafollicular C-cells in the thyroid gland secrete calcitonin. Calcitonin directly binds osteoclast receptors to arrest bone resorption and inhibits renal calcium reabsorption, returning blood calcium to normal. Option A.
questions.check: Independent check: PTH = hypercalcemic (raises calcium); Calcitonin = hypocalcemic (tones down calcium). Option A confirmed.

questions.source_name: NSEJS / Junior Science Biology · Q01 · MODEL · D2 (Score 4)
questions.stem:
In an investigation of plant cell water relations, cylindrical cores of uniform initial mass $m_0 = 5.00\text{ g}$ from Solanum tuberosum tuber tissue are incubated for 2 hours in a graded series of sucrose solutions at $20^\circ\text{C}$ ($293\text{ K}$). The percentage change in tissue mass $(\Delta m / m_0) \times 100\%$ is determined, intersecting the zero-net-flux baseline at an equilibrium sucrose concentration of $C = 0.25\text{ M}$.
[FIG-stem-bio-cell-water-potential]
Using the van 't Hoff equation for solute potential:
$$\Psi_s = -i C R T$$
(where ionization constant $i = 1.0$, gas constant $R = 0.0831\text{ L}\cdot\text{bar}/(\text{mol}\cdot\text{K})$, and $T = 293\text{ K}$), what is the water potential ($\Psi_w$) of the tuber tissue cells at incipient equilibrium, and what physiological state and turgor pressure ($\Psi_p$) do these cells attain when subsequently transferred to pure distilled water ($\Psi_w = 0\text{ bar}$)?
options: A: Psi_w = -6.09 bar; cells become fully turgid with Psi_p = +6.09 bar supported by the rigid cell wall
B: Psi_w = -6.09 bar; cells undergo osmotic lysis due to excessive hydrostatic pressure
C: Psi_w = 0 bar; cells remain flaccid with Psi_p = 0 bar
D: Psi_w = -12.18 bar; cells undergo incipient plasmolysis
questions.figure_note: Plant cell water potential equilibrium and turgor curve.

hints.prompt: H1 (Solute Potential Calculation): Apply van 't Hoff equation for C = 0.25 M.
H2 (Tissue Equilibrium): Relate external solution water potential to tissue water potential.
hints.text: At zero net mass flux in an open beaker (Psi_p = 0), Psi_w(tissue) = Psi_w(solution) = Psi_s = - 6.09 bar.

hints.prompt: H3 (Crux Move): Determine the final turgid equilibrium in pure water.
hints.text: Crux Move: In pure water (Psi_w = 0), water enters until inward cell wall pressure equals turgor pressure: Psi_w = Psi_s + Psi_p = 0 => Psi_p = + 6.09 bar. The cellulose wall prevents lysis.

questions.answer: Official Key: (A) Psi_w = -6.09 bar; cells become fully turgid with Psi_p = +6.09 bar supported by the rigid cell wall

2. Physical Model & Formulation: In an open container, Psi_p = 0 bar => Psi_w = Psi_s = - i C R T = -(1.0)(0.25)(0.0831)(293) = -6.09 bar. At equilibrium, Psi_w(tissue) = -6.09 bar.

B: Xylem vessels are living at maturity with thin cellulose walls operating by active ATP pumps; Sieve tube elements are dead at maturity with lignified walls operating by capillary action.

hints.text: Crux Move: Transpiration cohesion-tension creates negative tension in xylem, while Münch pressure flow creates positive turgor pressure in phloem. Option A.

Which of the following provides the strictly correct physical and biogeochemical justification for why ocean acidification threatens coral reefs and marine mollusks possessing calcium carbonate ($\text{CaCO}_3$) exoskeletons?

B: Elevated CO2 increases the pH of seawater, turning oceans alkaline and precipitating heavy metals onto coral surfaces.

However, anthropogenic chlorofluorocarbons (e.g. $\text{CF}_2\text{Cl}_2$) released into the troposphere migrate to the stratosphere and undergo photolytic cleavage by solar UV-C radiation:
$$\text{CF}_2\text{Cl}_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} \cdot\text{CF}_2\text{Cl} + \text{Cl}\cdot$$
The atomic chlorine radical ($\text{Cl}\cdot$) then catalyzes ozone destruction through a two-step cycle:
$$\text{Cl}\cdot + \text{O}_3 \to \text{ClO}\cdot + \text{O}_2$$
$$\text{ClO}\cdot + \text{O}\cdot \to \text{Cl}\cdot + \text{O}_2$$
Which of the following correctly identifies the net reaction of this catalytic cycle, and explains why a single chlorine radical can destroy upwards of $100,000$ ozone molecules?
options: A: Net reaction: O3 + O· -> 2 O2; Chlorine acts as a regenerated homogeneous catalyst that is not consumed in the overall reaction sequence.
B: Net reaction: 2 O3 -> 3 O2; Chlorine permanently binds to ozone molecules forming stable chlorinated polymers.
C: Net reaction: O2 + O· -> O3; Chlorine generates ultraviolet photons that accelerate ozone synthesis.

B: F1 plants are triploid and therefore produce completely sterile F2 seeds that cannot germinate under soil moisture.

questions.stem: According to the Dixon and Joly Cohesion-Tension theory for the ascent of sap in tall trees, the frictional and gravitational forces opposing sap ascent in a 100-metre-tall tree require a pulling tension of about 20 to 50 atm. Phenylthiocarbamide (PTC) tastes bitter to tasters. The non-tasting condition is caused by a
recessive allele. A non-taster woman marries a PTC-taster man. Their first two children are non-

questions.stem:
For fertilisation in angiosperms, pollen grains germinate and pollen tubes carry male gametes to
the ovules. Suppose a brinjal fruit is to contain 300 seeds. How many meiotic cell divisions are
required to produce the necessary female and male gametophytes?

hints.text: 1. Conceptual Model: In angiosperms, formation of each seed requires one viable megaspore (for the embryo sac) and at least one viable microspore (male gamete vehicle).

2. Quantitative Meiotic Count: To form 300 seeds: 300 functional megaspores require 300 megaspore mother cells to undergo meiosis (since 1 MMC yields 1 functional megaspore, 3 degenerate) = 300 meiotic divisions. For male gametes, 1 microspore mother cell yields 4 viable pollen grains; hence 300 pollen grains require 300 / 4 = 75 meiotic divisions.
3. Summation: Total meiotic cell divisions = 300 (female) + 75 (male) = 375 meiotic divisions. Hence Option B.

questions.stem:
In a type of carbon dioxide fixation, stomata remain open at night and CO2 first combines with
phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) to form four-carbon oxaloacetate. Which plant shows this ecological
adaptation?

2. Nocturnal Carboxylation: At night, atmospheric CO2 enters open stomata and is fixed by phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP) carboxylase into four-carbon oxaloacetate, then reduced to malate and stored in vacuoles.
3. Ecological Representative: Aloe is an obligate succulent CAM xerophyte exhibiting this nocturnal carboxylation strategy. Hence Option C.

questions.stem: Which statements explain root gravitropism?
options:
A: Statoliths in root-cap columella cells sediment in the direction of gravity and generate a signal for
asymmetric growth.

B: Auxin influx and efflux carriers create a differential auxin gradient between the upper and lower
sides, producing unequal growth and root curvature.

C: Curvature in gravity-stimulated roots can be explained by lateral redistribution of an inhibitor
formed in the root cap.
D: Proplastids containing carotenoids and protochlorophyll respond to gravity.

hints.text: 1. Conceptual Model: Plant root positive gravitropism involves graviperception, biochemical signal transduction, and asymmetric differential cell elongation.
2. Mechanistic Evaluation of Statements:
- Statement A is correct: Dense starch-rich amyloplast statoliths in columella cells sediment downward under gravity, triggering calcium and auxin signalling.

steps: 1. Conceptual Model: Plant root positive gravitropism involves graviperception, biochemical signal transduction, and asymmetric differential cell elongation.
2. Mechanistic Evaluation of Statements:
- Statement A is correct: Dense starch-rich amyloplast statoliths in columella cells sediment downward under gravity, triggering calcium and auxin signalling.

- Statement B is correct: Coordinated PIN and AUX/LAX auxin carrier relocalization establishes an asymmetric lateral auxin gradient across upper and lower tiers; in roots, supra-optimal auxin inhibits elongation on the lower side causing downward curvature.
- Statement C is correct: Classic physiological models (e.g. Torrey, Wilkins) hypothesized lateral redistribution of a root-cap growth inhibitor (e.g. abscisic acid or supraoptimal auxin).
- Statement D is incorrect: Graviperception statoliths are dense amyloplasts containing starch grains, not proplastids with carotenoids and protochlorophyll.
3. Synthesis: Statements A, B, and C are scientifically valid representations of the gravitropic response. Hence Options A, B, C.

B: Only ATP is generated; reducing power such as NADPH/NADH is not produced.
D: P680 is the active reaction centre.

hints.text: 1. Conceptual Model: Cyclic photophosphorylation operates when the cell demands ATP without concomitant generation of reducing equivalents (NADPH).

- Statement A is correct: The pathway is confined entirely to Photosystem I (PSI) located in non-appressed stroma thylakoids; PSII is not involved.

2. Mechanistic Verification of Characteristics:
- Statement A is correct: The pathway is confined entirely to Photosystem I (PSI) located in non-appressed stroma thylakoids; PSII is not involved.

- Statement B is correct: Excited electrons cycle from P700 through ferredoxin, cytochrome b6f, and plastocyanin back to P700, creating a proton gradient for ATP synthase without reducing NADP+ to NADPH.

Members of Cucurbitaceae, such as bottle-gourd, pumpkin, watermelon and muskmelon,
bear large fruits although their stems may be only finger-thick. What helps a large
quantity of food to be translocated from leaves to fruits for storage?

hints.text: 1. Conceptual Model: Long-distance translocation of photosynthetic assimilates requires robust, specialized vascular bundles.

3. Conclusion: Translocation is facilitated by bicollateral vascular bundles. Hence Option C.

In some birds, a black bird crossed with a white-feathered bird produces all
blue-plumaged chicks. If these blue birds are selfed, the offspring ratio will be:

The diagram shows chromatographic separation of pigments extracted from spinach
leaves. The sequence of pigment bands from below upwards is:
options: A: Chlorophyll b, Chlorophyll a, Carotenols and Carotenes

questions.stem: In the analysis of wastewater, Escherichia coli is used as:
options: A: A standard organism for performing a plate count
B: An indicator of faecal contamination of water
C: An indicator of the number of nitrogen-fixing bacteria in water
D: A measure of the amino-acid content of water

hints.text: 1. Conceptual Model: Coliform bacteria serve as microbiological indicator organisms to assess sanitary quality and potable water safety.

2. Diagnostic Indicator: Escherichia coli is a commensal bacterium inhabiting the lower intestine of warm-blooded animals. Because it is shed in large numbers in faeces, its presence in water samples reliably indicates recent faecal contamination and the probable presence of enteric pathogens.
3. Conclusion: E. coli is used as an indicator of water contamination by faecal matter. Hence Option B.

Acid rain damages soil and lakes and affects aquatic plants and animals. Which pH range
is most suitable for the survival of most aquatic biota?

hints.text: 1. Conceptual Model: Aquatic organisms maintain homeostatic osmoregulation and enzymatic function within narrow physiological pH windows.

2. Ecological Tolerance: The optimal pH range for freshwater teleost fish, aquatic invertebrates, and microflora is near neutral, between pH 6.5 and 7.5. Acidification below pH 6.0 mobilises toxic aluminium ions and impairs gill ion-exchange mechanisms.
3. Conclusion: The most suitable pH range is 6.5 to 7.5. Hence Option B.

questions.stem: If in a wheat mutant, the length of chromosome 1B was found to be 6.7 µm instead of 5.0 µm, approximately how many additional base pairs are incorporated in the mutant chromosome?

hints.text: 1. Conceptual Model: Standard double-stranded B-DNA has a helical rise per base pair of 0.34 nm = 0.34 * 10^-3 micrometres.

2. Quantitative Calculation: Initial chromosome length L1 = 5.0 micrometres, mutant length L2 = 6.7 micrometres. Net extension delta L = 6.7 - 5.0 = 1.7 micrometres = 1700 nm. The number of additional base pairs incorporated is N_bp = 1700 nm / (0.34 nm/bp) = 5000 bp = 0.5 * 10^4 bp.
3. Conclusion: The number of additional base pairs incorporated is 0.5 * 10^4 bp. Hence Option A.

questions.stem: Considering the following characteristics, identify the correct inheritance pattern from the given options. • Most affected individuals are male. • Affected sons result from female parents who are either affected or who are known to be carriers because they have affected brothers, fathers, or maternal uncles. • Affected daughters are born to affected fathers and either affected or carrier mothers. • The sons of affected mothers should be affected. • Approximately half the sons of carrier mothers should be affected.

hints.text: 1. Conceptual Model: In XY chromosomal sex determination, males are hemizygous for genes on the X chromosome and express any recessive allele carried on their maternal X.

2. Pedigree Criteria Evaluation: Male predominance occurs because a single mutant X allele confers the trait in males. Affected sons are born to carrier or affected mothers (inheriting mutant maternal X). Affected daughters require an affected father donating the mutant paternal X and a carrier or affected mother. All sons of affected homozygous mothers are affected. These classic criteria establish sex-linked recessive inheritance.
3. Conclusion: The inheritance pattern is sex-linked recessive inheritance. Hence Option C.

questions.stem: In a marine ecosystem with rich diversity of fauna, which of the following images would be a correct representation of the pyramid of biomass?
options: A: Upright pyramid with broad producer base and progressive tapering toward tertiary consumers
B: Spindle-shaped pyramid with constricted intermediate consumer tiers
C: Uniform columnar pyramid with equivalent standing biomass across trophic levels
D: Inverted pyramid of biomass (standing crop biomass of phytoplankton producers is smaller than zooplankton/fish consumers at any given instant)

hints.text: 1. Conceptual Model: An ecological pyramid of biomass depicts the standing crop dry weight of organisms across successive trophic levels at an instantaneous sampling point.

2. Marine Trophic Dynamics: In open marine ecosystems, microscopic phytoplankton primary producers have rapid turnover rates and short lifespans. Their instantaneous standing biomass is consistently smaller than the longer-lived zooplankton and fish feeding upon them, producing an inverted biomass pyramid.
3. Conclusion: An inverted pyramid of biomass correctly depicts the marine ecosystem. Hence Option D.

questions.stem: The transpiration pull is maximum under which of the following conditions?
options: A: Closed stomata, low light intensity and humid air
B: Open stomata, dry air and moist soil
C: Open stomata, dry air and dry soil
D: Open stomata, high humidity in air and moist soil

hints.text: 1. Conceptual Model: Transpiration pull is driven by the water potential gradient between moist soil, internal mesophyll air spaces, and ambient atmosphere.

2. Environmental Rate Factors: Open stomata minimize stomatal diffusion resistance; dry air maximizes the vapor pressure deficit and atmospheric water potential sink; moist soil supplies continuous water to roots to sustain cohesive xylem sap columns without cavitation.
3. Conclusion: Transpiration pull is maximum under open stomata, dry air, and moist soil. Hence Option B.

questions.stem: Curcuma longa, Azadirachta indica, Basmati Rice and Indian Ginseng are all related to which of the following concepts?

hints.text: 1. Conceptual Model: Biopiracy refers to the commercial exploitation or unauthorized patenting of indigenous biological resources and traditional knowledge by external entities without consent or equitable benefit-sharing.

Landmark Indian Case Studies: Curcuma longa (turmeric wound healing), Azadirachta indica (neem fungicidal properties), Basmati Rice (foreign strain patents), and Indian Ginseng (Ashwagandha) all represent historic international intellectual property disputes where India successfully contested or resisted unauthorized commercial claims.
3. Conclusion: These examples relate directly to the concept of biopiracy. Hence Option C.

questions.stem: Read the following criteria carefully. • Slow evolutionary change relative to similar entities. • Gross similarity to an ancestral fossil. • Very low taxonomic richness today compared to the past. • Phylogenetic inference of specific characters as plesiomorphic. • Phylogenetic inference of a genealogical divergence between other groups that diverged in the distant past. • Known in the fossil record before being discovered alive. These criteria can be used to categorise a group of organisms most probably into:

hints.text: 1. Conceptual Model: A living fossil is an extant organism that has retained ancestral plesiomorphic anatomical traits over evolutionary epochs with slow morphological divergence (bradytely), exhibiting low modern taxonomic richness compared to its fossil record.

2. Criteria Alignment: Gross morphological similarity to ancestral fossils, low modern diversity, plesiomorphic character suite, and historical recognition in fossil strata prior to the discovery of living specimens (e.g. Latimeria, Limulus, Ginkgo) define living fossils.
3. Conclusion: The specified criteria categorize the group as living fossils. Hence Option B.

questions.stem: Choose the correct statements from the following options.
options: A: A robust adaptive immune response is initiated using weakened forms of the bacterium known as live attenuated vaccines.
B: Administration of a killed or chemically inactivated virus can trigger a weaker adaptive immune response, but it can be strengthened with booster doses.
C: A conjugate or multivalent component always reduces immunogenicity of the vaccine.
D: Inclusion of alum, cytokines and/or lipids always reduces the immune response to a vaccine.

hints.text: 1. Conceptual Model: Vaccines induce immunological memory through exposure to pathogen-specific immunogens without causing full pathology.

2. Vaccine Design Evaluation: Statement (a) is true: live attenuated vaccines replicate in host tissues, establishing robust and durable adaptive humoral and cell-mediated immunity. Statement (b) is true: killed or inactivated vaccines trigger weaker adaptive responses and typically require booster doses. Statement (c) is false: conjugate designs enhance T-dependent immunogenicity of polysaccharide antigens. Statement (d) is false: adjuvants like alum and lipids are included to potentiate and enhance the immune response.
3. Synthesis: Statements (a) and (b) are correct. Hence Options A, B.

questions.stem: The minimum energy required to exist, that is, the energy required to perform chemical reactions even when a person is at rest, is called the basal metabolic rate (BMR), which accounts for about 50 to 70 per cent of the daily energy expenditure in most sedentary individuals. It is influenced by many factors. Some statements are made about these factors. Choose the correct statements from the following options.
options: A: Thyroid hormone decreases metabolic rate.
B: Growth hormone increases metabolic rate.

hints.text: 1. Conceptual Model: Basal Metabolic Rate (BMR) represents the minimum baseline rate of energy expenditure by an endothermic organism at complete physical and emotional rest.

2. Physiological Factor Evaluation: Statement (a) is false: thyroid hormones (T3 and T4) increase oxygen consumption and stimulate BMR (calorigenic effect). Statement (b) is true: growth hormone accelerates protein synthesis and tissue anabolism, elevating metabolic rate. Statement (c) is false: fever raises core temperature and accelerates biochemical reactions (Q10 effect), increasing BMR. Statement (d) is true: prolonged malnutrition prompts adaptive metabolic depression to conserve endogenous energy reserves, lowering BMR.
3. Conclusion: Statements (b) and (d) are correct. Hence Options B, D.
